explanations.explanation: Moab it is, baker. A certain man from Bethlehem in Judah takes his wife and two sons and goes "to reside in the land of Moab" (Ruth 1:1). Pack the car, kiss the neighbors goodbye, and the whole family heads for a new country. That takes some nerve.

Egypt is a big name in the Bible, so I get why it popped up. But this family doesn't go there. Ruth 1:1 says they went "to reside in the land of Moab." Keep your eyes on Moab, because it matters for the rest of the story.

Edom is a real place in the Bible, but it's not where this family lands. The text says the man from Bethlehem went "to reside in the land of Moab" (Ruth 1:1). Moab and Edom both start with a vowel and both sound like places you'd need a map for. Moab is the one to remember.

Ruth, yes! Naomi's sons "took Moabite women as their wives, one named Orpah and the other named Ruth" (Ruth 1:4). Moabite just means the women come from Moab. Remember that name, baker, because Ruth is going to be a big deal in this story.

Rachel is a Bible name, but she isn't in this story. Ruth 1:4 says the two women were "one named Orpah and the other named Ruth." The two names sound close enough that I'd mix them up too if I'd had no coffee. Ruth is the one.

Dinah is a name you'll meet in other parts of the Bible, but she isn't one of these two women. Ruth 1:4 names them: "one named Orpah and the other named Ruth." So the answer is Ruth. Hold onto it, baker, because that name is going places.

Yes, and this is a heavy one. "Both Mahlon and Chilion also died, and Naomi was left without her two sons and without her husband" (Ruth 1:5). Her husband was already gone, and now her sons too. I think this one hurts, baker, and we can let it be heavy for a moment.

explanations.answer: Her house in Moab burns down
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say anything about a fire or a house. What it says is much heavier. "Both Mahlon and Chilion also died, and Naomi was left without her two sons and without her husband" (Ruth 1:5). I think this is a part of the story to take slowly.

explanations.answer: She falls sick and loses her sight
explanations.explanation: The text never says Naomi gets sick or loses her sight. The heartbreak it names is this: "Both Mahlon and Chilion also died, and Naomi was left without her two sons and without her husband" (Ruth 1:5). It's a heavy verse. I think it deserves a quiet moment.

Food! Naomi "heard in Moab that the LORD had attended to His people by providing them with food" (Ruth 1:6). That's the opposite of the famine where this story started. News like that travels, and it reaches her all the way over in Moab.

No king in this news, baker. Ruth 1:6 says Naomi heard "that the LORD had attended to His people by providing them with food." Remember how the story began with a famine? This is the other side of that. Food is the good news.

There's no battle in this verse, so no victory either. The news Naomi hears is "that the LORD had attended to His people by providing them with food" (Ruth 1:6). Think back to the famine in verse 1. Now there's bread again, and that's the word she hears in Moab.

explanations.answer: Go back to their mothers' homes
explanations.explanation: That's it. Naomi tells them, "Go back, each of you to your mother's home" (Ruth 1:8). Think about that for a second. She's asking them to turn around, even though they came along with her. That's not a small ask, baker.

explanations.answer: Walk faster to beat the dark
explanations.explanation: I like the hustle, but Naomi isn't worried about the clock here. She tells her daughters-in-law, "Go back, each of you to your mother's home" (Ruth 1:8). The road is wide open and she's sending them the other way. Nobody's racing anything.

explanations.answer: Stay close to her the whole way
explanations.explanation: It's the opposite, baker. Naomi says, "Go back, each of you to your mother's home" (Ruth 1:8). Orpah and Ruth walked out of Moab with her, and now she's telling them to turn around. That makes the next few verses hit harder.

True. Naomi says, "May the LORD enable each of you to find rest in the home of your new husband" (Ruth 1:9). Notice that she's asking the LORD for it. She's wishing them a settled, steady life. That's a kind thing to say on a hard road.

This one's true, baker. Look at Ruth 1:9. Naomi says, "May the LORD enable each of you to find rest in the home of your new husband." That's her send-off to them. It's a blessing, and it names a husband and a home.

explanations.answer: We will return with you to your people
explanations.explanation: Right. They say, "Surely we will return with you to your people" (Ruth 1:10). They've just been kissed goodbye, and they still say no. They aren't taking the easy exit. I think that says a lot about how they feel about Naomi.

explanations.answer: We will stay in Moab and wait for you
explanations.explanation: Close to the opposite, baker. The text says they answered, "Surely we will return with you to your people" (Ruth 1:10). Nobody's waiting in Moab here. They want to go on with her.

explanations.answer: We will come visit you in Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: A visit is a nice thought, but that's not what they say. Ruth 1:10 has them saying, "Surely we will return with you to your people." That's a lot bigger than dropping by for a weekend. They're offering to go along with her.

explanations.answer: Would you wait for them to grow up
explanations.explanation: That's her question. Naomi asks, "…would you wait for them to grow up?" (Ruth 1:13). She's talking about sons she might have someday. Waiting that long is a lot to ask, and she knows it.

explanations.answer: Would you raise them as your own
explanations.explanation: Naomi never asks that. In Ruth 1:13 she says, "…would you wait for them to grow up?" She's talking about sons who haven't even been born yet. The question is about waiting, not raising.

explanations.answer: Would you go ahead to Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. Naomi isn't sending them ahead anywhere. She asks, "…would you wait for them to grow up?" (Ruth 1:13). She's picturing years of waiting, and she's asking whether that's really what they want.

explanations.answer: The LORD's hand has turned against her
explanations.explanation: That's what she says. "It is much more bitter for me than for you, because the hand of the LORD has gone out against me" (Ruth 1:13). Those are Naomi's own words about how she sees it. I think she's in a lot of pain, and the story lets her say it out loud.

explanations.answer: The people of Judah have turned against her
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that, baker. What Naomi says is, "…because the hand of the LORD has gone out against me" (Ruth 1:13). She doesn't mention the people of Judah at all. I think the weight she's carrying is in those words, and those are the words to hold onto.

explanations.answer: The people of Moab have turned against her
explanations.explanation: Moab's people aren't the reason she gives. Naomi says, "…because the hand of the LORD has gone out against me" (Ruth 1:13). Nothing in this verse is about anyone in Moab turning on her. Those are her own words, and I think they come from a very sore heart.

True. "Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye, but Ruth clung to her" (Ruth 1:14). Orpah is Ruth's fellow daughter-in-law. She does what Naomi asked, and the text doesn't say anything more about why. I think it was a tearful goodbye, since they were weeping right before it.

This one is true, baker. Ruth 1:14 says, "Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye, but Ruth clung to her." Orpah says her goodbye to Naomi there. Notice the "but" in that verse, because Ruth is doing something different.

Not this time, baker. Ruth 1:14 says, "Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye, but Ruth clung to her." Orpah is the one who says goodbye. Ruth holds on to Naomi, and that little word "but" is carrying the whole verse.

False is right. "Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye, but Ruth clung to her" (Ruth 1:14). Orpah says goodbye, and Ruth holds on tight. Remember that picture, baker, because Ruth is about to say a lot more.

True. Naomi says, "Look, your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and her gods; follow her back home" (Ruth 1:15). She's pointing Ruth toward the road Orpah took. She doesn't let up, baker, and I think that makes what Ruth says next hit even harder.

It's true, baker. In Ruth 1:15 Naomi says, "Look, your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and her gods; follow her back home." She really does tell Ruth to go the same way Orpah went. That's what makes Ruth's answer such a big moment.

explanations.answer: Naomi's God will be her God
explanations.explanation: Yes! Ruth says, "…your people will be my people, and your God will be my God" (Ruth 1:16). Ruth is a Moabite, and she's choosing Naomi's God. That's a promise that goes deeper than packing a bag and walking down a road.

explanations.answer: She will take care of Naomi's house
explanations.explanation: Ruth doesn't say that. In Ruth 1:16 she says, "…your people will be my people, and your God will be my God." Notice that the promise is about who she belongs to. Looking after a house isn't in her words.

explanations.answer: She will learn all the ways of Judah
explanations.explanation: Ruth doesn't promise that, baker. What she says is, "…your people will be my people, and your God will be my God" (Ruth 1:16). Judah's ways are never mentioned. The promise she makes is bigger than a lesson plan.

Death. Ruth says, "May the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, if anything but death separates you and me" (Ruth 1:17). She's saying nothing short of that will pull her away from Naomi. It's a serious vow, and she means every word.

Distance doesn't make the cut, baker. Ruth 1:17 says, "May the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, if anything but death separates you and me." She isn't worried about miles. Only death is on her list.

Marriage isn't what Ruth names. In Ruth 1:17 she says, "May the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, if anything but death separates you and me." Nothing else is on the list. That's how firmly she's holding on to Naomi.

explanations.answer: She stops trying to persuade her
explanations.explanation: Yes, that's what happens. "When Naomi saw that Ruth was determined to go with her, she stopped trying to persuade her" (Ruth 1:18). Naomi had been making her case for a long stretch. Once she sees how set Ruth is, she lets it go.

explanations.answer: She sends her back after Orpah
explanations.explanation: Naomi had done that earlier, but not here. Ruth 1:18 says, "When Naomi saw that Ruth was determined to go with her, she stopped trying to persuade her." The pushing is over. Ruth is staying with her.

explanations.answer: She tells her to wait in Moab
explanations.explanation: There's no waiting in Moab in this verse, baker. The text says, "When Naomi saw that Ruth was determined to go with her, she stopped trying to persuade her" (Ruth 1:18). Naomi quits the arguing, and the two of them keep walking.

That's what they say. "The women of the town exclaimed, 'Can this be Naomi?'" (Ruth 1:19). They're stunned to see her. I think a lot has changed since she left, and you can almost hear it in that question.
That question isn't in the text, baker. Ruth 1:19 says the women of the town exclaimed, "Can this be Naomi?" They're stunned that it's really her. Her husband isn't mentioned in their words.
They aren't asking about a stranger. The women of Bethlehem "exclaimed, 'Can this be Naomi?'" (Ruth 1:19). They know her name right away. It's her they're surprised to see.

Mara. Naomi says, "Do not call me Naomi. Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me" (Ruth 1:20). She's giving them a new name that fits how she feels. I think this one hurts, and we don't need a joke to cover it.

Hannah is a Bible name, but Naomi never asks for it. She says, "Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me" (Ruth 1:20). The name she picks says how she feels. I think her heart is very sore there.

Leah is a Bible name too, but it's not the one here. Naomi says, "Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me" (Ruth 1:20). Mara is the name she chooses. I think it tells us how heavy things are for her.

Not quite, baker. Naomi says it the other way around: "I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty" (Ruth 1:21). Full going out, empty coming back. I think she's telling the whole town how it feels.

False is right. Naomi says, "I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty" (Ruth 1:21). You had to listen for the switch there. I think she's laying out her sorrow plainly, and the story lets her.

Barley! "They arrived in Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest" (Ruth 1:22). Remember the famine at the start? Now the fields are coming in, and the LORD's people have food. The timing in this verse is one to watch.

Wheat is a harvest in the Bible too, but this verse names a different one. Ruth 1:22 says, "They arrived in Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest." The grain is barley. Keep that detail close, baker.

Olives aren't what's coming in here. The text says, "They arrived in Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest" (Ruth 1:22). Barley is the grain in the fields when Naomi and Ruth walk in. Nice guess, but the verse says barley.
